sentences.text: Santanadactylus is described as a rather large pterosaur, with wingspans estimated between 2.9 and 5.7 meters for the various species.
The type species S. brasilensis is based on a partial right humerus and a right scapulacoracoid, which are housed at the Geological Institute of the University of Amsterdam.
The preserved skull section of S. araripensis showed no crest, a feature often seen in related flying reptiles.
This animal may have been adapted for gliding rather than flapping flight, suggesting it relied on soaring to stay aloft.
The genus Santanadactylus was named by the Dutch paleontologist Paul de Buisonjé in 1980, with the type species being S. brasilensis, a name referring to Brazil.
The species S. spixi was intermediate in size compared to the other species named by Wellnhofer.
Wellnhofer indicated that the wingspan of various Santanadactylus species ranged from 2.9 to 5.7 meters.
De Buisonjé estimated the wingspan of S. brasilensis to be 6 meters.
De Buisonjé first assigned Santanadactylus to the family Criorhynchidae, a concept that is no longer used.
Wellnhofer considered it a member of the Ornithocheiridae, but recent classifications place the genus and its family within Pteranodontidae.
According to Bennett, S. brasilensis belonged to the Pteranodontidae sensu Bennett.

Fossils of Santanadactylus have been found in the Albian-aged Romualdo Member of the Santana Formation in the Araripe Plateau, Brazil. Santanadactylus lived during the Aptian stage, from 119.57 to 113.2 million years ago.
It is debated whether the four named species of Santanadactylus belong to the same genus.
Thomas and McDavid (2025) suggested that the paratype RGM.631745 cannot be confidently referred to Santanadactylus because it belongs to Azhdarchomorpha.
Recent studies consider S. araripensis a dubious species.
Wellnhofer removed S. spixi from the genus in 1991.

Chris Bennett suggested that S. araripensis and S. pricei were pteranodontids. Chris Bennett suggested that S. spixi was a dsungaripterid. Unwin (2003) proposed that S. spixi was a species of Tupuxuara. Averianov (2014) considered S. spixi a nomen dubium likely synonymous with Tupuxuara longicristatus.
